chapter: Childhood, first teachers and the Wilberforce Collegians
title: Summers at the Roseland: Fletcher's original band personnel
summary: Every summer Horace sat by Fletcher at the Roseland. He describes the reeds (Redman, Hawkins, Bailey), Kaiser Marshall, tuba, and the brass section.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: The only experience that I got which I was gonna get to -- every summer I would look forward to going to New York, and I would go right to the Roseland, I'd sit right by my brother on the stand and pick up pointers and things to go back to school in September again. And he would help me out this way, and I would watch every guy. I had my notebook and everything -- would watch the way his original guys did. You know the original band that Fletcher had consisted of Don Redman, Coleman Hawkins, and Buster Bailey. That was his reed section. I know them real well as if it were yesterday. Those three sounded like six, because they didn't double on instruments, they tripled. They did everything. Don Redman played everything. He used to go around to pawn shops and pick up old kazoos and everything because his daddy was an old band master, you know, and Don could play all these things, and some of Fletcher's earlier records had these different sounds on 'em. And that was from Don Redman from the pawn shops. And Coleman Hawkins played the saxophone, the bass sax, the baritone, and Buster Bailey played the tenor, and of course the clarinet. That was the reed section. Then he had Kayser Marshall on the drums that
sock cymbal invented the (unintelligible). He's the one that started this.

He had a guy named Escudero that played the tuba, and he was a foreigner, excellent tuba man. This was before the days of the great late John Kirby. And his brass section consisted of a guy that was three-fourths Indian called Big Green from Nebraska, Omaha, Nebraska. I'm telling you these things for a point. And he played trombone. One of the greatest trombonists that I've ever heard play a waltz. Then he had a trumpet player by the name of Elmer Chambers. He had another trumpet player named Scotty. (Howard Scott-ed.) -- he had 3 to start with. This was his brass section (inaudible). And later came another guy that got into that section which -- I think his name might be familiar -- Louis Armstrong.
I believe I've heard of him, somewhere along the way.
